notes:
WHY BE MORAL? (Section D: Moral Decision-making, Chapter 2)

OPENING QUOTE
- "The heart has its reasons, of which reason knows nothing." (Blaise Pascal)

WHY BE MORAL? - THE SEAT BELT EXAMPLE
- We rarely think about WHY we behave the way we do.
- Hugh and Riona both wear seat belts when driving - the SAME action, but DIFFERENT motivations.
- Hugh: "so that if I crash, my head will not go out through the windscreen." He is motivated by PERSONAL SAFETY.
- Riona: "so that if the Garda stop me, I will not get a fine and penalty points." She is motivated by FEAR OF BREAKING THE LAW and the punishment that follows.

STARTING POINT
- The way we think things out shapes the decisions we make.
- People can reach the SAME conclusion to a moral dilemma for DIFFERENT reasons.
- People of the same culture and the same religion can reach VERY DIFFERENT conclusions.
- Why? Because people have different ways of being moral. Being moral is a HUMAN ACTIVITY: it is a person, with a particular personality and experience, who is being moral in a certain situation - "and we all do things a little differently!"
- People also live moral lives because of their religious beliefs, so we must look at how faith influences morality.

REASONS FOR BEING MORAL
- There are both HUMAN and RELIGIOUS reasons for being moral.
- Four main reasons: HAPPINESS, GROWTH, LAW, SERVICE TO SOCIETY.
- Happiness: being moral means achieving happiness. When we do the right action, we achieve happiness for ourselves and for others.
- Growth: being moral leads to personal growth. Doing the right action is good for me in the long run; when we act correctly we are becoming good people.
- Law: being moral is following a law. Right and wrong have been enshrined in law and it is our duty to follow the moral law. The motive for action is REWARD/PUNISHMENT.
- Service to society: being moral means being of service to society, transforming our world so it is better for everyone. The morally correct action brings JUSTICE TO ALL and ENHANCES THE LIFE OF THE COMMUNITY.
- None of these ways is complete in itself. Our motives are often a MIXTURE of all of them, but they help us understand how people think. Our reasons are more complex than we might think.
- The exercise in the chapter lists actions (driving on the left, not doing drugs, visiting an elderly aunt, paying taxes, not cheating on a spouse, giving to famine relief, not telling racist jokes, standing up to bullying, following Arsenal FC) and possible reasons (a rule of my church; the law of the land; right for me living my faith; good for the community; makes me feel better; makes others happy).

FAITH AND MORALITY
- For those who believe in God, faith shapes their view of the world. Moral behaviour is seen as:
- a way of following God, becoming the person God wants us to be;
- obeying God's laws on how we relate to others and to our world;
- a way of responding to God's love for us.
- All major world religions - Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism and Hinduism - have teachings on ethics; some very similar, some different.
- St Thomas Aquinas put it simply: "Seek good, avoid evil." But our lives are a complex mixture of good and evil.
- A person's faith affects how they judge between good and evil. A faith community's common belief system gives a set of principles by which to live.
- KEY LINE: "A genuinely religious person will be a moral person; a moral person need not necessarily be a religious person."

WAYS OF APPROACHING MORALITY (Higher Level only)
- Three approaches: DEONTOLOGICAL, TELEOLOGICAL and RELATIONAL ethics.
- For each: definition, how it works in practice, and how a Christian might use it.

DEONTOLOGICAL ETHICS
- From the Greek word DEON, meaning DUTY or OBLIGATION.
- States there is an OBJECTIVE moral theory - a law, a code of behaviour - that is NOT CHANGED over time or situation, which sets out how we should act.
- Views morality primarily in terms of DUTY, LAW or OBLIGATION.
- Judges an act NOT by its consequences but by whether it is right or wrong by the law. The law is true in all circumstances.
- Example: a deontologist would not break a red traffic light because it is against the law - even in the middle of the night with no one around!
- Questions this person asks: What is the law? What is my duty?
- Examples: "I declare and pay my taxes because that is my duty and it is what the law demands." "I do not smoke in school because it is against the rules and I have a duty to look after my health."
- "I was only doing my duty" reflects deontological reasoning.
- For the Christian: the moral law is inspired by the Word of God. The Ten Commandments are an example of a moral code in scripture. It is a Christian's duty to follow the commandments and the moral teachings of Jesus.

TELEOLOGICAL ETHICS
- From the Greek word TELOS, meaning END or GOAL.
- Good actions lead toward our FULFILMENT and ULTIMATE HAPPINESS. The key to what is right is WHAT WILL HAPPEN AS A RESULT of my action.
- Views the moral life in terms of the goal, end or good to be achieved.
- Examples: "I declare and pay my taxes because I seek a fair opportunity for all in life." "I do not smoke in school because it will damage my health, slow me down in sports, and maybe get me in trouble."
- For the Christian: the ultimate goal of Christian life is to BE WITH GOD. An act is good if it leads toward that goal; evil if it prevents one from reaching it.

RELATIONAL ETHICS
- Gives primacy to the desire to live in RIGHT RELATIONSHIP with the world around us, with ourselves and with God.
- Views the moral life as a set of relationships: with NEIGHBOUR, WORLD, SELF and GOD.
- Examples: "I declare and pay my taxes because I have a responsibility toward the wider community in which I live." "I do not smoke in school because it is unhealthy for me and for others."
- For the Christian: the motive to be good comes from one's RELATIONSHIP WITH CHRIST.

MORAL LAW - ITS DIFFERENT EXPRESSIONS
- Natural Law: written in the heart, within every person; using our reason, it enables us to know good and evil.
- Revealed Law: the law given in scripture - the OLD LAW of the Hebrew scripture and the NEW LAW of the gospel.
- Civil Law: the law of the State.

NATURAL LAW THEORY
- Definition: by use of our REASON, any person can come to know the natural law, WRITTEN ON OUR HEARTS, which helps us discern good from evil.
- Attraction: within all of humanity a rational agreement on the moral law is possible.
- It is NOT written down anywhere. Everyone has access to it through reason. Our moral duties can be found by REFLECTION ON HUMAN NATURE.
- Example: parents care for their children because they know in their hearts it is right - they follow the natural law.

NATURAL LAW IN LITERATURE AND THOUGHT
Sophocles' Antigone
- The plot is the drama between the WRITTEN laws of the State and the UNWRITTEN laws, which have a higher moral claim.
- Polynices rebelled against his uncle, KING CREON. By the king's order he was left to die (lie unburied) outside the city walls; anyone who buried him would be put to death.
- ANTIGONE, Polynices' sister, defied Creon and buried him, because she felt there is a greater law than the law of the State.
- Quote: "I did not think your edicts wrong enough to overrule the unwritten, unalterable laws of God and heaven, you being only a man." (Antigone to Creon)
The Stoics
- Established in Greece around 300 BCE, later spread to Rome.
- Called on people to live a good life IN ACCORDANCE WITH NATURE. Their code is called STOIC ETHICS.
- Almost all classical moral philosophers of the West have adapted some form of Natural Law theory.

THOMAS AQUINAS AND NATURAL LAW
- Hugely significant influence on Catholic moral thought; developed and used Natural Law theory.
- By using reason to reflect on our human nature we can discover:
- the specific ends to which we naturally tend;
- the general ends that God has planned for us.
- Aquinas called this understanding of God's plan for us the NATURAL LAW. It is how we rational people PARTICIPATE IN GOD'S ETERNAL LAW.
- "The Natural Law is nothing other than the light of understanding placed in us by God; through it we know what we must do and what we must avoid." God gave this light or law at creation.
- Looking at nature we see the purpose for which all is created. An act is good if it helps achieve that purpose.
- We are created so that we can: LIVE, REPRODUCE, ACQUIRE KNOWLEDGE and WORSHIP GOD.
- Good acts help us achieve these ends; evil is what stops us achieving them.
- Examples:
- We are made to learn, so it is good to teach people - it helps them to fulfilment.
- We are created as equals, so it is wrong to discriminate against anyone for any reason.
- The earth was created for us to live on and care for, so destroying it through pollution is against the natural law.

MODERN CRITICISM OF NATURAL LAW THEORY
- Too many interpretations: because it is not written, people reach different conclusions about how to use it. Moral philosophers HOBBES, BUTLER, HUME and KANT all differ in how they view human nature.
- Too rigid: if natural law is seen as given and fixed in nature, it can never change. Some argue it is better to say we are GIFTED in our nature so we can use reason to work out what is good IN OUR TIME - then natural law can adapt to changing times.
- Too physicalist: some versions look only at the PHYSICAL reality of human nature, not at other goods. A person is also a PSYCHOLOGICAL, SPIRITUAL and SOCIAL being.
- The "worker's manual" image: the maker of a machine knows best how it works, so we need the manual (natural law as the blueprint for our machine). This is called NATURAL LAW PHYSICALISM. Problem: it limits natural law to the physical/biological - the person is more than a machine!

OVERALL VALUE OF NATURAL LAW
- The Second Vatican Council continued to teach about natural law (Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, GAUDIUM ET SPES, n.16), but also stressed that Christians must let FAITH, GRACE and the GOSPEL shape their moral life.
- Gaudium et spes 16 key lines: "Deep within their consciences men and women discover a law which they have not laid upon themselves and which they must obey." Its voice calls them "to love and to do what is good and to avoid evil... do this, shun that." "They have in their hearts a law inscribed by God." "Conscience is the most secret core and the sanctuary of the human person. There they are alone with God whose voice echoes in their depths." The law is "fulfilled in the love of God and of one's neighbour." Through loyalty to conscience, Christians are joined to others in the search for truth.
- Greatest value: natural law is OPEN TO ALL PEOPLES, of any faith or none, to know right and wrong by reflecting with reason on human nature.
- Exercise: Romans 2:14-16 (does the writer agree with a natural law?). Reflection: CCC Part Three, Chapter Three, "God's Salvation: Law and Grace".

SUMMARY
- There are different reasons for acting morally; motivation and method shape decision-making.
- Being moral means seeking good and avoiding evil.
- Being religious means one's life is directed by one's faith, which guides one's actions.
- Teleological ethics seeks to achieve a good end; Deontological ethics follows the moral law; Relational ethics seeks to live in right relationship with all.
- Natural Law theory: through reason we can know what is morally right.

KEY TERMS (one-line definitions)
- Deontological ethics: morality as duty or obligation to an unchanging law; acts judged by the law, not consequences.
- Teleological ethics: morality judged by the end or goal; right actions lead to fulfilment and happiness.
- Relational ethics: morality as living in right relationship with neighbour, world, self and God.
- Moral Law: the law of right and wrong, expressed as Natural, Revealed and Civil Law.
- Natural Law: the law written on our hearts that anyone can know through reason.
- Revealed Law: the law given in scripture - Old Law (Hebrew scripture) and New Law (gospel).
- Civil Law: the law of the State.

rows.model_answer: As a way of following God and becoming the person God wants us to be; as obeying God's laws on how we relate to others and our world; and as a way of responding to God's love for us.

rows.prompt: Explain deontological ethics and give one example.
rows.model_answer: Deontological ethics, from the Greek 'deon' (duty), says there is an objective moral law that does not change with time or situation. An act is judged by whether it is right or wrong by the law, not by its consequences. For example, a deontologist would not break a red light even at night with no one around.

rows.prompt: What is teleological ethics? Give an example.
rows.model_answer: Teleological ethics, from the Greek 'telos' (end or goal), judges actions by their result: good actions lead to fulfilment and happiness. For example, 'I do not smoke because it will damage my health and slow me down in sports.' For the Christian, an act is good if it leads to the goal of being with God.

rows.prompt: Give an example of how a Christian might follow a relational way of doing ethics.
rows.model_answer: Relational ethics is about living in right relationship with neighbour, world, self and God. A Christian acts well because of their relationship with Christ - for example, paying taxes out of responsibility to the wider community.

rows.prompt: Name and explain the three expressions of the moral law.
rows.model_answer: Natural Law is written in every heart and known through reason. Revealed Law is given in scripture: the Old Law of the Hebrew scripture and the New Law of the gospel. Civil Law is the law of the State.

rows.prompt: How did Thomas Aquinas describe natural law?
rows.model_answer: Aquinas said that by using reason to reflect on human nature we discover the ends we naturally tend to and those God planned for us. He called this the natural law, the way rational people participate in God's Eternal Law - 'the light of understanding placed in us by God'. We are made to live, reproduce, acquire knowledge and worship God; good acts help us reach these ends.

rows.prompt: Why do some thinkers say Natural Law theory can be too rigid?
rows.model_answer: If natural law is seen as given and fixed in nature, it can never change. They argue it is better to say we are gifted in our nature so we can use reason to work out what is good in our time, letting the natural law adapt to changing times.

rows.prompt: Outline the deontological, teleological and relational approaches to morality and show how a Christian might use each. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Deontological ethics comes from the Greek 'deon', meaning duty or obligation. It holds there is an objective moral law that does not change over time or situation. An act is judged not by its consequences but by whether it is right or wrong by the law; a deontologist would not break a red light even at midnight with no one around. The person asks: what is the law, what is my duty? For the Christian, the moral law is inspired by the Word of God, as in the Ten Commandments, and it is one's duty to follow them and the moral teachings of Jesus. Teleological ethics comes from 'telos', meaning end or goal. Good actions lead to fulfilment and ultimate happiness, so what is right depends on what will happen as a result. For example, 'I pay my taxes because I seek a fair opportunity for all.' For the Christian the ultimate goal is to be with God: an act is good if it leads there and evil if it blocks it. Relational ethics gives primacy to living in right relationship with neighbour, world, self and God. For example, 'I do not smoke in school because it is unhealthy for me and for others.' For the Christian the motive to be good comes from one's relationship with Christ.
rows.marking_scheme: Each approach: meaning/origin 2 marks + explanation/example 2 marks + Christian use 2 marks (x3 = 18); overall coherence 2 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain the theory of Natural Law, referring to Thomas Aquinas, and discuss modern criticisms of it. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Natural Law theory says that by using our reason any person can know the natural law written on our hearts, which helps us tell good from evil. It is not written down; we find our moral duties by reflecting on human nature. For example, parents care for their children because they know in their hearts it is right. Thomas Aquinas, a huge influence on Catholic moral thought, said reason reveals the ends we naturally tend to and the ends God has planned for us. He called this the natural law, the way rational people participate in God's Eternal Law: 'the light of understanding placed in us by God'. We are made to live, reproduce, acquire knowledge and worship God; good acts help us reach these ends. So teaching is good because we are made to learn, discrimination is wrong because we are created equal, and pollution is wrong because the earth is ours to care for. Critics say there are too many interpretations: Hobbes, Butler, Hume and Kant differ on human nature. Some say it is too rigid, and should adapt to our time. Others say it is too physicalist, treating the person like a machine with a manual, when a person is also psychological, spiritual and social. Still, its great value is that it is open to people of any faith or none.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: reason; written on hearts; not written down; parents example; Aquinas - ends, Eternal Law, 'light of understanding'; four ends; examples; criticisms - interpretations (Hobbes, Butler, Hume, Kant), too rigid, too physicalist/machine manual; value - open to all.

rows.prompt: How does Sophocles' play Antigone illustrate the idea of a natural law? (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The key to the plot of Antigone is the conflict between the written laws of the State and the unwritten laws, which have a higher moral claim. Polynices rebelled against his uncle, King Creon, and by the king's order he was left outside the walls of the city. Anyone who buried him would be put to death. Antigone, his sister, defied Creon and buried him, because she believed there is a greater law than the law of the State. She told Creon: 'I did not think your edicts wrong enough to overrule the unwritten, unalterable laws of God and heaven, you being only a man.' This shows the idea of natural law: a moral law that is not written down but which people know within themselves, and which is higher than any civil law made by a ruler.
rows.marking_scheme: Story of Creon, Polynices and Antigone 4 marks; quote or paraphrase 2 marks; link to unwritten higher law / natural law 4 marks.

rows.prompt: 'A genuinely religious person will be a moral person; a moral person need not necessarily be a religious person.' Discuss, with reference to the reasons people have for being moral. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: People have both human and religious reasons for being moral. The chapter names four main human reasons. Happiness: doing right brings happiness to ourselves and others. Growth: doing right is good for us in the long run, as we become good people. Law: we follow the moral law out of duty, with reward and punishment as motive. Service to society: we transform the world, bringing justice to all and enhancing community life. None is complete in itself, and our motives are usually a mixture. The seat belt example shows Hugh acting for his safety and Riona from fear of a fine - neither reason is religious, yet both act well. So a person can be moral without religion. Natural Law theory supports this: anyone, of any faith or none, can know right and wrong by reason. For a believer, however, faith shapes their view of the world. Moral behaviour becomes a way of following God and becoming the person God wants us to be, obeying God's laws, and responding to God's love. All major religions - Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism and Hinduism - have ethical teaching. Aquinas summed it up: 'Seek good, avoid evil.' A genuinely religious person, whose life is directed by faith, will therefore live morally.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: four reasons (happiness, growth, law, service to society); mixture of motives; seat belt example; natural law open to all; faith - following God, obeying God's laws, responding to God's love; world religions; Aquinas.

rows.prompt: What did the Second Vatican Council teach about the natural law and conscience in Gaudium et spes 16? (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The Second Vatican Council continued to teach about the natural law in the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World, Gaudium et spes, n.16. It says that deep within their consciences men and women discover a law which they have not laid upon themselves and which they must obey. Its voice calls them to love, to do what is good and to avoid evil, telling them inwardly 'do this, shun that'. They have in their hearts a law inscribed by God, and their dignity rests in observing it. Conscience is 'the most secret core and the sanctuary of the human person', where they are alone with God. This law is fulfilled in the love of God and neighbour, and loyalty to conscience joins Christians to others in the search for truth. The Council also stressed that Christians must let faith, grace and the gospel shape their moral life.
rows.marking_scheme: Law within conscience not self-made 3 marks; 'do this, shun that'/law inscribed by God 2 marks; conscience as sanctuary 2 marks; fulfilled in love/search for truth 1 mark; faith, grace and gospel 2 marks.
